hero.title: Alloys
hero.lead: In your previous studies you learned about metals, their properties, and how they differ physically and chemically. Here you will learn about another type: alloys — their definition and the story of their discovery through history.

objectives: Define an alloy and give an example of one.
Give a historical overview of humanity's discovery of alloys, from iron meteorites to bronze.
Explain why ancient humans preferred bronze over pure copper.

content.heading: 💡 8-4 Alloys
content.html: Dear student, in your previous studies you learned about metals, their properties, and how they differ physically and chemically. Here you will learn about another type: alloys, and their kinds.

content.label: 📌 Definition — Alloy
content.html: An alloy is a mixture made up of a metal and another element, where most alloys contain at least one of two components: a large amount of the main or base metal, and smaller amounts of other components, which may be metals or nonmetals such as carbon and silicon.

content.descriptionHtml: Move the slider to explore the historical progression of humanity's discovery of alloys, from iron meteorites to bronze.

ruleBoxes.html: In prehistoric times, humans discovered iron meteorites and gold-silver mixtures at the bottom of riverbeds — the first alloys humans found ready-made in nature.

labels.ev0_text: In prehistoric times, humans discovered iron meteorites and gold-silver mixtures at the bottom of riverbeds — the first alloys humans found ready-made in nature.
labels.ev1_text: The first alloy made by humans is believed to be bronze, made of copper and arsenic.
labels.ev2_text: Tin was discovered and combined with copper, producing a good grade of bronze.
labels.ev3_text: The manufacture of tools, jewelry, and weapons from bronze began, since it is harder than copper and more suitable for casting and molding.

content.html: Humans discovered alloys in nature during prehistoric times, and these alloys included iron meteorites and gold-silver mixtures at the bottom of riverbeds. The first alloy made by humans is believed to be bronze, made of copper and arsenic; tin was then discovered and combined with copper, producing a good grade of bronze, after which the manufacture of tools, jewelry, and weapons began, since bronze is harder than copper and more suitable for casting and molding into useful shapes.

content.label: 🔍 Explanation — Why did ancient humans prefer bronze over pure copper?
content.html: Bronze is harder than pure copper and more suitable for casting and molding into useful shapes, which is why the manufacture of tools, jewelry, and weapons from bronze began instead of from pure copper.

The methods of forming alloys differ from one alloy to another, since these methods depend on the melting point of the materials that make it up, as well as their freezing point; the properties of the materials making up an alloy can be controlled through heat treatments for each material.

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson Summary
items: An alloy is a mixture made up of a large amount of a base metal, and other elements (metals or nonmetals such as carbon and silicon) in smaller amounts.
Humans discovered alloys in nature before recorded history: iron meteorites and gold-silver mixtures at the bottom of riverbeds.
The first alloy made by humans is believed to be bronze (copper + arsenic), which then developed with the addition of tin to become harder and more suitable for casting and molding than pure copper.
The methods of forming alloys depend on the melting and freezing points of their materials, and their properties can be controlled through heat treatments.
